Mr. Snyder, a Republican who left office in January after term limits prevented him from seeking re-election, has not been charged with any crimes. But search warrants released Monday revealed that investigators had seized the cellphone he used while in office and other mobile devices, as well as devices belonging to dozens of members of his administration.
The warrants, first
reported by The Associated Press
, signaled that prosecutors examining the Flint water crisis in recent months have been scrutinizing Mr. Snyder.
“The team is currently in the process of obtaining this evidence through a variety of means, including search warrants,” Solicitor General Fadwa Hammoud, a member of the prosecution team, said in a written statement. “The team is also conducting a thorough review of existing and newly received evidence pertaining to the Flint water crisis.”
Flint, a financially challenged city with nearly 100,000 residents, became synonymous with government failure after an emergency manager appointed by Mr. Snyder changed the city’s drinking water source to the Flint River in 2014 in an effort to save money. Within weeks, residents began complaining that their water smelled funny, tasted foul and was causing illnesses.
The residents were correct: Flint’s water was tainted by lead and linked to a deadly Legionnaires’ outbreak. But government officials, including members of Mr. Snyder’s administration, dismissed those complaints for months and assured residents that their tap water was safe. Errors by state, local and federal officials
exacerbated the crisis
and delayed the response.
As the scope of the crisis became clear in 2016,
Mr. Snyder apologized
for not taking action sooner and promised state assistance. Attempts to reach Mr. Snyder on Monday were not immediately successful.
“I’m sorry most of all that I let you down,” Mr. Snyder said in 2016. “You deserve better. You deserve accountability. You deserve to know that the buck stops here with me. Most of all, you deserve to know the truth, and I have a responsibility to tell the truth.”
But even as he promised help — and as members of his administration were charged with felonies — Mr. Snyder denied any criminal wrongdoing. An investigation started by the state attorney general led to charges against 15 people in state and local government, including a member of Mr. Snyder’s cabinet and
emergency managers he appointed
. Through it all, residents continued to ask whether Mr. Snyder would be prosecuted.
“Just because you’re the governor of a state does not make you immune to facing accountability for your actions and inactions,” said Melissa Mays, a Flint resident and water activist, after the new search warrants seeking information about Mr. Snyder and others were revealed.
Ms. Mays, who is among the many Flint residents who still does not drink tap water, said she thought the search warrants would “open a lot of doors to some answers and hopefully justice.”
Still, it remained unclear whether the inclusion of Mr. Snyder’s iPhone and iPad in the search warrants signaled a new focus by prosecutors or just a broad review of records. The investigative team has been overhauled since Attorney General Dana Nessel, a Democrat, took office early this year. Her predecessor was a Republican. Another Democrat, Gretchen Whitmer, took office as governor, replacing Mr. Snyder.
Records show that the investigators also have sought records from several other officials, including some who had been charged with crimes and many who had not. Included in the search warrant were former Lt. Gov. Brian Calley, who has not been charged, and Nick Lyon, the former health and human services secretary, who is accused of involuntary manslaughter.

You can pinpoint
the exact moment when “The Angry Birds Movie 2” decides it’s going to stop being one kind of animated sequel and becomes another. The
original 2016 film
, based on
the popular video games
, imagined an island full of flightless birds being suddenly terrorized by green porcine, egg-stealing invaders. The new movie starts in a constant state of sniping between Bird Island and Piggy Island, with each group playing elaborate, cruel pranks on one another.
Then, a third, even more menacing island emerges — Eagle Island, run by a brilliant but embittered eagle named Zeta (voiced by Leslie Jones), who sends destructive ice-balls toward both pigs and birds.
In most cases, a sequel would either expand upon or regurgitate the previous setup, so one might expect yet another foray — this time led by the first film’s hero Red (Jason Sudeikis) and his former nemesis, the pig chieftain Leonard (Bill Hader) — into the new island. And that is exactly what happens.
But as soon as the group arrives on Eagle Island, “Angry Birds 2” mostly tosses story, character and sense aside, and opts for a go-for-broke style of humor. The hoops our heroes jump through become increasingly surreal and hilarious.
Highlights include a bit involving an attempt to steal an eagle’s ID card at a urinal, and a breakdance battle that comes out of nowhere and is resolved in even stranger fashion.
Those hoping for a sharply-scripted, well-proportioned work may be disappointed, but one might ask them why they’re seeing a film called “The Angry Birds Movie 2” in the first place.

Back Story
The
wintry storms raging around the U.S.
this week aren’t, thankfully, bringing with them the plunging temperatures of the
recent polar vortex
. That brutal blast of cold offered a reminder of the one temperature where the Fahrenheit scale agrees with Celsius: minus 40.
Both scales address two major calibration points (freezing and boiling), but divide the temperature range between them in differently sized degrees. There are a lot more degrees in Fahrenheit, and the two intersect at just that one point.
Daniel Fahrenheit
, an 18th-century physicist and inventor, made his scale for a mercury-in-glass thermometer that was the first accurate and practical way to measure temperature.
He used a frigid mix of ice, water and salt to define zero degrees. Then he borrowed and refined other reference points from an existing scale, which is how other commonly used points ended up with untidy values like 32 for water’s freezing point and 212 for its boiling point.
Anders Celsius
, whose lifetime overlapped Fahrenheit’s, set those reference points at 100 for freezing and zero for boiling. Those were reversed after his death.
Kenneth Chang, a science reporter who says he “hates the Fahrenheit scale — and miles and ounces and those other British units that even the British dropped decades ago,” wrote today’s Back Story.
